name: Erik Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most of my work these days is new connections. Brookfield's growing like mad, there's a new housing estate every year on what used to be fields, and we put in the poles, run the overhead lines out from the main road and hook up the transformers so the houses get power. I'm in the depot at seven, we load the truck, and by eight we're on site dodging diggers. It's honest work and you can see what you've built at the end of it, which I like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mud, and the builders changing the plans after we've dug the holes. Last month they moved a whole road two metres and we had to shift four poles we'd put in the week before. And the early starts, at fifty-eight, I feel them more than I used to.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Carol works mornings at the pharmacy on the high street. Our two are grown, one's a teacher, one's in sales. We're a bit stretched at the moment, honestly. We've got a car loan and Carol needed dental implants last year, which wiped out what we had, so there's maybe a couple of weeks in the bank. Brookfield depot pays a bit under the city rate, and there's not another line company for forty miles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. My daughter set me up with one of those AI apps and it's useful for some things, but it's not going to run a line through a muddy field. I'd say it at the depot, maybe in the family chat, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan holds. Work to sixty-six, pay off the car in two years, and try to get a bit of a cushion back. Nothing clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Once the car's paid off in 2028, that money goes straight into savings. I might use the app a bit more for the boring stuff, like checking a regulation, but I always double-check with the foreman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, honestly, that I don't have to rethink anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you use the AI app for now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bits and pieces. I asked it last month what size of cable we'd need for a run of thirty houses, just to see if it'd match what the engineer said. It was close, but not right, so I don't trust it with anything that matters yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money, plain and simple. If the car broke down tomorrow, we'd be on the credit card. That's got nothing to do with AI and everything to do with last year.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised, because the AI app my daughter set up is useful for some things but won't run a line through a muddy field. I'd say it at the depot and in the family chat.
S0.think: Privately, my plan holds: work to sixty-six, pay off the car in two years and rebuild a cushion. Nothing clever.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and plans to move the car loan payment into savings once it's paid off in 2028. Uses the AI app a little for checking regulations but double-checks with the foreman.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased not to have to rethink anything.
S0.quote: It was close, but not right, so I don't trust it with anything that matters yet.
S0.fieldNote: Erik's test of the AI app against the engineer's figures sums him up: open to trying, slow to trust. His stress is about money from last year's dental bill, not technology. He frames his whole life as a plain plan to sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense to get on with it sensibly. Train people, change what needs changing, don't panic. I'd say that at the depot, and I'd mean it, because panic never fixed anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm all right for the actual line work, but the planning side might change a lot. If software starts laying out the new estates and sending us the plans, fine, as long as the plans are better than the builders' ones. My worry is that they'd need fewer of us on each crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for the first crews to try any new kit, then put my name down for training. I'd keep up the car payments and try to put twenty a week aside. And I'd talk to the foreman about which way things were going, because he usually knows six months before we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, nothing more. It's like a forecast that says rain later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would be most affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Dan, our ground man. He does the digging and the fetching, and that's the sort of thing a machine could do. He's forty and has three kids, so I'd worry about him more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to try things first. Has that served you well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. When the battery tools came in, I waited a year and by then they'd fixed the problems. The lads who jumped first had tools dying halfway up a pole.

S1.say: I'd say get on with it sensibly: train people, change what needs changing and don't panic. I'd say it at the depot and mean it.
S1.think: I think the line work itself is safe, but software could take over the planning of new estates. My real worry is that they'd need fewer of us on each crew.
S1.do: Waits for the first crews to try new kit, then signs up for training. Keeps up the car payments, saves about twenty a week and asks his foreman which way things are heading.
S1.feel: Mildly uneasy, like a forecast of rain later.
S1.quote: The lads who jumped first had tools dying halfway up a pole.
S1.fieldNote: Erik's steady approach is backed by real experience with the battery tools. He worries more about his ground man with three kids than about himself. He trusts his foreman as an early warning system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government had better have a plan, because two years is no time at all. I'm not one to shout, but I'd want to hear from someone in charge what happens to people my age. I'd say that at the depot and to our local representative if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me. I'd be sixty, with a car loan and nothing put by. Even if the robots take a while to get onto the estates, the company would stop hiring and start looking for people to let go, and the older ones on lower pay are easy pickings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd sell the car and buy something cheap outright, to get rid of the loan. I'd ask about any early retirement deal and do the sums with Carol at the kitchen table. And I'd ask the football league if they need more referees on Saturdays, because that's thirty or forty a match, and I've done it as a volunteer for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years' warning give you any room at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. It's enough time to get rid of the car loan and that's about it. It's not enough to save a cushion on what I earn, and it's certainly not enough to learn something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we might need a hand for a while, which is the last thing a father wants to say. My son would say, Dad, of course. My daughter would start sending me articles about it, she does that.

S2.say: I'd say the government had better have a plan, because two years is no time. I'd want to hear what happens to people my age, at the depot or from our local representative.
S2.think: It scares me, because I'd be sixty with a car loan and nothing saved. The company would stop hiring and start letting people go, and older workers on lower pay are easy pickings.
S2.do: Sells the car to clear the loan and buys a cheap one outright. Works out early retirement figures with his wife and asks the football league for paid refereeing on Saturdays.
S2.quote: The older ones on lower pay are easy pickings.
S2.fieldNote: Two years leaves Erik no time to build a cushion, so his plans are about cutting debt and finding small extra income. He'd turn his volunteer refereeing into paid work. Asking his children for help is the hardest part for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get it right, if they start now. People should be trained, and older workers need a fair deal. I'd say that calmly, at work and to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three. That's closer to my pension, and the car would be paid off. I'd still be short, but I could see a way through if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the car's paid off, every penny goes into savings, maybe two hundred a month. In the first year I'd also try the new tools once the other crews had, and I'd ask about a role supervising whatever machines come in. And I'd keep the refereeing as a bit on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's manageable. I'd feel like I had some say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time to clear debt and build a little cushion. Two years is a cliff. Five years is a steep hill, and I can walk down a hill if I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving the trade before it changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if something solid came up. A friend works as a site supervisor for a building firm, and he's said they need people who understand power. I'd look at it, but I wouldn't jump until I'd seen it work for someone else.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get it right if they start now, with training and a fair deal for older workers. I'd say that calmly to anyone who asked.
S3.think: Five years takes me to sixty-three, with the car paid off. I'd still be short, but I could see a way through if I'm careful.
S3.do: Puts about two hundred a month into savings once the car is paid off and tries new tools after other crews have. Asks about a supervising role for the new machines and keeps paid refereeing on the side.
S3.feel: Anxious but manageable, with a sense of some control.
S3.quote: Two years is a cliff. Five years is a steep hill, and I can walk down a hill if I'm careful.
S3.fieldNote: Five years matches Erik's pace: time to clear debt and see new tools proven. He'd consider leaving the trade for a building firm, but only after seeing someone else do it. His calm, careful tone stays the same throughout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and there's no excuse for anyone not being ready. I'd say it at the depot, and probably tell the younger ones to start thinking now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-eight, so I'd have retired. The car would be long paid off, and if I'm sensible we'd have a bit put by. It'd be my kids and the younger lads I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working to sixty-six, save hard once the car's done, and use the new tools as they come in. I'd tell Dan, our ground man, to look at training now while he's got time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, mostly for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'if I'm sensible'. How likely is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. We've said it before and something always comes up, like the teeth. But with ten years and the car gone, I'd like to think we'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to get his tickets for the new machines as soon as they're offered. He's got three kids and twenty-five working years left, and he needs to be on the right side of it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning and there's no excuse for not being ready. I'd tell the younger ones at the depot to start thinking now.
S4.think: I'd be sixty-eight and retired, with the car long paid off and maybe a bit saved. My thoughts would be with my kids and the younger lads.
S4.do: Keeps working to sixty-six, saves hard once the car is paid off and adopts new tools as they arrive. Urges his ground man to start training for the new machines now.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, mostly for others.
S4.quote: We've said it before and something always comes up, like the teeth.
S4.fieldNote: Erik admits his saving plans have failed before when life got in the way. With ten years he turns to advising a younger colleague. He stays measured and practical throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is a fair early retirement deal for people near the end, and a clear plan from the government so we're not all guessing. Something you can sit down at the kitchen table and do sums with.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to have built half a town's power and wonder if anyone will need you. Every estate in Brookfield, I've had a hand in it. Funny thing to be scared about losing.

headlineQuote: Every estate in Brookfield, I've had a hand in it. Funny thing to be scared about losing.
portrait: Erik Baker is a fifty-eight-year-old lineworker who connects new housing estates in a fast-growing commuter town, on a depot rate a bit below the city. A car loan and his wife's dental implants have left them with about two weeks of savings. He's pragmatic and careful, tests AI tools now and then but double-checks them, and waits for others to try new kit first. He is calm when AI fizzles, mildly uneasy with steady change and alarmed by AGI in two years, which he calls a cliff. More warning time turns it into a hill he can walk down, by clearing debt and saving.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be sixty with a car loan, no savings and little time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: A fair early retirement deal for people near the end, and a clear government plan he can work through at the kitchen table.
